title: History of the Ontology of Art

summaries.example: Imagine a song saved on a phone, written in a notebook, and played by three different bands. Are these four things the same artwork, or are they copies, performances, or clues that help us experience the song? Philosophers use questions like this to think about what an artwork really is.
summaries.summary: The ontology of art asks a basic question: what are artworks? A painting seems to be a physical object, but a song can be performed by different people, and a poem can appear in many copies. Philosophers have offered several answers. Some say artworks are real things independent of anyone’s beliefs. Others say an artwork has a special kind of being, depends on imagination or attention, or is connected to an artist’s actions and history. Some distinguish the artwork from its physical vehicle, such as a canvas, score, or performance. Others think there is no one kind of thing called an artwork, or that we can speak about art without claiming that artworks are separate entities. The history described in the entry focuses especially on debates from the nineteenth century onward.
key_ideas: Philosophers ask whether artworks exist and what sort of things they are.
A painting, a song, and a play may not exist in exactly the same way.
Some theories connect artworks with physical objects, while others connect them with minds, imagination, actions, or abstract patterns.
A performance or copy may help us experience a work without being identical to the work itself.
There is no single answer accepted by all the philosophers discussed.
summaries.why_it_matters: These questions change how we think about originals, copies, performances, restoration, and artistic creation. They also help explain why a song is not simply one recording and why a painting may be connected both to a unique object and to qualities that a copy can share. Studying these ideas makes us more careful about what we mean when we say that an artwork exists.

important_terms.definition: The study of what kinds of things are real and how they exist.
The view that artworks are real and do not depend entirely on what people think or feel about them.
The physical thing that helps us experience an artwork, such as paint on a canvas or sounds in a performance.
The ability of a work, such as a song or poem, to have more than one instance or performance.

questions_to_think_about: If a song can be played many times, what stays the same each time?
Is a painting only the painted object, or is there more to the artwork?
Could an artwork exist when nobody is looking at it?
Can a copy ever be just as good as an original?

summaries.example: Suppose two composers, working in different historical settings, independently write scores with exactly the same notes. One theory may treat them as the same sound pattern; another may say they are different works because the composers’ intentions and contexts differ. This case shows why the ontology of art must consider not only physical features but also authorship, performance conventions, and artistic history.
summaries.summary: The history of art ontology examines what sort of entities artworks are and how they persist, are identified, and relate to physical objects and experiences. Realists hold that artworks are real independently of beliefs, but other theories give them distinctive modes of being, such as subsistence, artistic existence, or aesthetic existence. Imagination-centered views connect artworks with make-believe, perception, and the relation between perceptible foregrounds and imagined backgrounds; some of these views risk making a work intermittent. Idealists reverse the usual priority of the physical world and treat artistic reality as fundamentally mental or experiential, while critics worry that this confuses an experience with its object and makes art too private. Eliminativists deny that artworks need to be included in fundamental ontology. Further debates concern monism, the distinction between a work and its vehicle, and whether works are abstract types, norm-kinds, artifacts, indicated structures, or actions. The entry presents these proposals as an evolving set of disputes rather than a settled theory.
key_ideas: Art-ontology asks whether artworks exist, how they are individuated, whether they are created or discovered, and whether they can be destroyed.
Realist theories treat artworks as independent entities; other theories assign them distinctive modes of being or make them dependent on imagination, experience, or artistic activity.
The work–vehicle distinction addresses the fact that a score, canvas, recording, or performance may present a work without simply being identical to it.
Repeatability creates pressure for abstract-object theories, while creation and destruction create pressure against treating works as timeless abstractions.
Monism claims that all artworks share one ontological category, but performance works, paintings, improvisations, and oral works seem to resist a single classification.
Competing proposals include Platonism, types and tokens, norm-kinds, artifacts, indicated structures, action types, and action tokens.
summaries.why_it_matters: Our answer affects how we understand originals and replicas, musical performances, literary texts, restoration, artistic intention, and the possibility of destroying a work. It also reveals that ordinary expressions such as “the symphony,” “the painting,” or “the poem” may cover several related things: a physical object, a repeatable pattern, a performance, an action, or an object of appreciation. Art ontology therefore connects metaphysics with the actual practices of making, presenting, interpreting, and evaluating art.

important_terms.definition: The branch of metaphysics that investigates what exists and the kinds or modes of being entities have.
The view that artworks are entities whose existence does not depend on anyone’s actual or possible beliefs or responses.
A theory holding that some artworks are abstract entities, such as repeatable types, rather than spatiotemporal objects.
The distinction between a repeatable pattern or kind and a particular occurrence of that pattern.
A distinction between the artwork and the material object, event, or medium through which it is experienced.
The claim that a work exists only while it receives a suitable kind of perceptual or imaginative attention, though its physical basis remains.
A kind whose instances may be correct or flawed according to standards set by the kind.
The strategy of avoiding commitment to artworks as entities while retaining useful ordinary talk about art.

questions_to_think_about: If a musical work is abstract, how can it literally have audible properties?
Does a perfect copy share the identity of a painting, or only some of its artistic functions?
Should the historical context of an artwork determine which work it is?
Can an artwork be created if the pattern or structure it uses already existed?
Would ordinary talk about artworks survive an eliminativist theory?

summaries.example: Think about a school play. The script is one thing, the actors’ performance is another, and the stage props are still another. Yet we may say that all of them are connected to the same play. If another class performs the script, is it the same artwork, a new artwork, or another instance of it? Different philosophers answer differently because they disagree about what makes an artwork the artwork it is.
summaries.summary: The ontology of art is the philosophical study of what artworks are. A physical painting may seem easy to identify, but music, literature, theater, photography, and other arts raise harder questions. A song can have many performances, a poem can have many copies, and a play can be connected to a script, a performance, and a history of artistic choices. Philosophers have responded in several ways. Realists say artworks are real and do not depend completely on people’s opinions. Other theories give artworks special kinds of being or make them depend on imagination and aesthetic attention. Some thinkers distinguish a work from its vehicle—the material thing that presents it. Others argue that artworks are patterns, types, norm-kinds, artifacts, actions, or historically situated entities. A further disagreement concerns monism: whether every artwork belongs to one ontological category. Finally, eliminativist views suggest that we can discuss art without treating artworks as separate entities in our deepest account of reality.
key_ideas: The central question is not whether art is valuable, but what sort of thing an artwork is.
A work may be different from its physical vehicle, even though the vehicle lets people experience it.
Some philosophers think works are independent and real; others connect them with imagination, experience, or artistic activity.
Repeatable works such as songs and poems create different problems from singular works such as particular paintings.
Monism is challenged by the variety of paintings, performances, improvisations, and oral works.
The entry surveys theories rather than choosing one final answer.
summaries.why_it_matters: These debates help explain everyday disagreements about originals, copies, performances, recordings, and restorations. They also show why an artwork cannot always be identified simply by pointing to a physical object. Thinking about ontology encourages us to separate several questions: what we encounter, what we appreciate, what the artist made, and what makes an artwork continue to be the same work over time.

important_terms.definition: The study of what exists and what kind of existence different things have.
The idea that artworks are real even though people’s beliefs or feelings do not create them.
The physical object or event through which we encounter an artwork, such as a canvas, score, recording, or performance.
A pattern or kind that can have particular occurrences, called tokens.
A particular occurrence of a type, such as one printed copy or one performance of a work.
The view that all artworks belong to one basic kind of entity.
The view that an artwork may depend on imagining, pretending, or attending to it as art.
The proposal that no special artwork entities are needed in our basic account of reality.

questions_to_think_about: Is a performance of a play the play itself, or a way of presenting it?
What makes two performances performances of the same work?
Can a work exist while nobody is attending to it?
If two artists make indistinguishable objects in different situations, have they made the same artwork?
Does a work need an artist’s intention in order to exist?
